title: What Kind of HVAC System Do I Have?
h1: What Kind of HVAC System Do I Have? How to Tell
description: Not sure what HVAC system you have? Learn to tell a furnace and AC from a heat pump, packaged unit, mini-split or wall furnace, and where to find model info.
quick_answer: Most Southern California homes have a split system: a gas furnace in the attic, garage or hall closet paired with an outdoor AC unit. Others have a heat pump, a packaged unit on the roof or side yard, ductless mini-splits or a wall furnace. The equipment's data plate and your thermostat settings will tell you which one you have.
body:
Knowing your system type helps when you call for service, shop for filters, compare replacement options or just figure out why your heat feels the way it does. You don't need tools to find out. A quick walk around the house usually answers it.

What are the common types of HVAC systems in SoCal homes?

Split system with gas furnace and AC

This is the most common setup locally. The furnace is indoors, usually in the attic, garage or a hall closet, and has a metal flue pipe running up through the roof. An outdoor condenser unit sits in the side or back yard. Ductwork carries air to registers in each room.

Heat pump split system

It looks almost identical from outside, but the outdoor unit heats and cools. Indoors, there's an air handler instead of a gas furnace, so you won't see a gas line or flue pipe. Many heat pump thermostats have an "emergency heat" or "aux heat" setting.

Dual-fuel system

A heat pump outdoors paired with a gas furnace indoors. The heat pump handles most heating, and the furnace takes over when needed.

Packaged unit

Everything is in one cabinet outside, either on the roof or on a pad beside the house, with ducts running into the home. You'll find these on some single-story homes, condos and manufactured homes.

Ductless mini-split

Small indoor units mounted high on walls or in the ceiling, connected to an outdoor unit by refrigerant lines. Common in additions, ADUs, garage conversions and older homes without ducts.

Wall or floor furnace

Many older homes in San Diego and Orange County still have a gas wall furnace in a hallway or a floor furnace with a grate in the floor. These heat a small area and have no ducts and no central AC.

How can you tell which one you have?

  1. Find the indoor unit. Check the attic, garage, hall closets and laundry room. Look for a cabinet with a filter slot and ducts attached.
  2. Look for a gas line and flue. A gas pipe going into the unit and a metal vent pipe out the top mean it's a gas furnace.
  3. Check outside. A condenser or heat pump sits on a pad in the yard. If it's the only unit and has ducts connected directly to it, it's a packaged system.
  4. Look at the thermostat. Settings like "emergency heat," "aux heat" or "heat pump" point to a heat pump.
  5. Read the data plate. The metal or sticker label on each unit lists the brand, model number and serial number. Model numbers often indicate whether it's an AC or heat pump.

What information should you write down?

Snap a photo of the data plate on both the indoor and outdoor units. These details help any technician:

  • Model and serial numbers, which also reveal the manufacture date
  • Refrigerant type, such as R-22, R-410A or a newer refrigerant
  • Filter size, printed on the edge of the current filter
  • Where the equipment is located and how easy it is to reach

If the label shows R-22, the system is older and uses a refrigerant that's no longer produced. That's worth knowing before any big repair.

How old is your system?

The serial number usually encodes the year and sometimes the week it was built. Formats vary by manufacturer, so the easiest way is to give the number to a technician or look it up on the manufacturer's site. Knowing the age helps you plan: most AC units and heat pumps last roughly 10 to 15 years, and furnaces often last longer.

Why does your system type matter?

It affects your maintenance needs, your filter size, how you should use the thermostat and what your replacement options are. Heat pumps benefit from service in both spring and fall. Attic furnaces need clear, safe access for repairs. Wall furnaces can't be paired with central AC without adding ducts or going ductless.

If you're still not sure what you've got, our HVAC technicians can identify the system during a tune-up, tell you its age and condition, and explain your options if an upgrade makes sense.
faqs: How do I know if I have a heat pump or an air conditioner?

Check the thermostat for an emergency or auxiliary heat setting, look for a gas line and flue on the indoor unit, and read the outdoor unit's data plate. If heat comes on and the outdoor unit runs in winter, you have a heat pump.
Where is my furnace usually located?
In Southern California, furnaces are usually in the attic, the garage or a hallway closet. Basements are rare here. Look for a metal cabinet with a filter slot and ducts attached.
What size filter does my system use?

The size is printed on the edge of the filter currently installed, such as 16x25x1. Some systems have filters in a return grille in the ceiling or wall rather than at the furnace. Write the size down so you always buy the right one.
